Article Title: War of NH blockades in Manipur: Kuki women body moves Supreme Court
Article Text:
CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.

NEW DELHI: Blockading NHs in Manipur by ethnic groups to inconvenience opponents is common but the Supreme Court on Friday took serious note of the humanitarian crisis such actions unleash after an NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population in there without food and healthcare.Senior advocate Anand Grover, appearing for Kuki Women Organisation for Human Rights, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the NH-2 and supply routes to Kangpokpi has been blocked by Naga groups creating a crisis for the population and requested the SC to direct the Centre and the state to reopen the NH. “The state just can’t sit and do nothing,” he complained.Intervening in the matter, an Imphal-based NGO – International Meitei Organization – through senior advocate Ngangom Junior Luwang said the Kukis had been “responsible for blocking all major NHs in Manipur since May 2023, after the Kuki-Meitei ethnic clashes began, and now they are playing the ‘victim card' when faced with the consequences of such blockades by another ethnic group.”“It is a matter of record that since May 3, 2023, members of the community, of which the petitioner is a part of, have been blocking all major NHs in Manipur - NH2 (Imphal to Dimapur), NH-37 (Imphal to Silchar), and NH-102 (Imphal to Moreh) and except for intermittent flow of goods vehicles through extortion rackets reportedly perpetuated by Kuki community,” the NGO alleged.CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.When Luwang welcomed the CJI’s suggestion, Grover immediately offered the petitioner organisation’s cooperation but wondered who would bring the Naga group to the talks.SC issued notices to the Centre, Manipur govt and National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) and said the larger public interest demands removal of blockade of all NHs in the state as well as restoration of supply to Kangpokpi district.It said Grover assured that his client in cooperation with social organisations would work towards the same and recorded similar sentiments expressed by Luwang on behalf of the Meitei NGO. It asked all the parties to suggest modalities for reopening all NHS without engaging in blame games. It posted the matter for further hearing after two weeks.
Article Summary: CJI Surya Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other. An NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population without food and healthcare.

Article Title: SC concerned by continuance of derogatory witch-hunting practice
Article Text:
The Supreme Court of India

NEW DELHI: More than 75 years of the Constitution coming into force, the derogatory practice of witch-hunting that targets defenceless women due to prejudice, suspicion, superstition and irrational fear, continues in the country, the Supreme Court lamented while upholding life term for two who murdered a woman in a tribal village of Odisha in Feb 1998.A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria said the facets of the case had a disturbing impact on the court as a defenceless woman was branded a practitioner of witchcraft and was brutally assaulted in front of her daughter. “What effect it must have had on the daughter of the deceased who had to witness her mother being killed in the most brutal way,” the bench wondered.Writing the judgment, Justice Mishra said the malady of with-hunting continues to plague sections of our society, where prejudice, superstition, and irrational dear supersede the rule of law and constitutional morality.“The brutality associated with witch-hunting extends far beyond the act of killing; where victims mostly women are subjected to torture, beatings, sexual violence and social ostracization. In such a situation, superstitious beliefs or fears are given precedence leading to vulnerable women becoming victims of collective hostility,” he said.IN Feb 1998, in the remote village of tribal inhabited Sundergarh district, one Manobodha Naik’s daughter died, and family members claimed that she died because of witchcraft practice of one Puni Naik.Hearing this Udai Oram dragged Puni Naik to Naik’s house and with his associate, mercilessly assaulted her with sticks leading to her death. The trial court had convicted the duo in 2002, but the Orissa HC took two decades to uphold the conviction and life sentence.Justices Mishra and Anjaria said, “Sometimes in the most difficult situations, it often becomes an easy escape to blame a woman for the acts she did not commit, thus reflecting a deeply rooted social prejudice that often seeks scapegoats rather than solutions. In such situations, what can be given an ascendency is ‘reason’ for reason is the only virtue that stands as a bulwark against collective irrationality.”SC said the Constitution guarantees equality, promotes fraternity and envisages citizens to adopt scientific temperament to rid the society of derogatory practices against women. “Despite this, practices such as witch-hunting continue to persist within a few sections of our society. A Constitutional democracy such as ours cannot survive; wherein such derogatory practices continue to elude the principles of rule of law and Constitutional morality,” it said.
Article Summary: Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria said the facets of the case had a disturbing impact on the court as a defenceless woman was branded a practitioner of witchcraft. “What effect it must have had on the daughter of the deceased who had to witness her mother being killed in the most brutal way,” the bench wondered.

Article Title: ‘Have to isolate dimaagi Naxals’: PM Modi in Independence Day speech from Red Fort

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday called for the isolation of what he described as "dimaagi Naxals", while asserting that armed Naxalism and Maoist violence were "breathing its last" in the country.Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on the 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said the country needed to remain vigilant against those who continued to propagate Naxal ideology even as armed Maoist violence declined."Armed Naxals are gone, but 'intellectual Naxals' still lurking; we must be vigilant," PM Modi said.PM Modi said Naxalism and Maoism had held large parts of the country in their grip for decades and caused the loss of thousands of lives."In the 21st century, it is imperative that we eliminate the decades-old challenges that have held the country back. Naxalism and Maoism have destroyed the future of millions of young people. They have snatched away the young sons of countless mothers and shattered the dreams of families across the country. For nearly four decades, Naxalism had held large parts of India and a huge section of its population in its grip, ruling through the barrel of a gun and tearing the Constitution to shreds.More than 3,500 of our police and security personnel sacrificed their lives while protecting ordinary citizens. Naxalism had turned the land red with blood."He said the government had made eliminating Naxalism a priority after coming to power in 2014."When you gave us the opportunity to serve in 2014, we resolved on that very day to free the country from Naxalism."PM Modi said the security situation in Naxal-affected areas had changed, with development and government initiatives reaching regions that had earlier witnessed violence."Today, I am happy to say that Naxalite and Maoist violence no longer has the strength to sustain itself and is breathing its last. We are moving towards completely eliminating it. In areas where the bullets of Naxalites once rang out, where the soil was once stained with blood, today the same Naxal-affected regions are witnessing the tricolour of development, trust and endeavour flying high as they move towards becoming Naxalism-free. "PM Modi's remarks came as part of his wider Independence Day address, in which he outlined the government's priorities and challenges facing India as it moves towards the goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for the isolation of what he described as "dimaagi Naxals" He said armed Naxalism and Maoist violence were "breathing its last" in the country. PM Modi's remarks came as part of his wider Independence Day address. He outlined the government's priorities and challenges facing India.

His latest address came on India's 80th Independence Day.Also read: 80th Independence Day - A throwback at PM Modi's signature Red Fort turbans Nehru, India's first prime minister, holds the record for the longest uninterrupted run of Independence Day addresses, having delivered 17 consecutive speeches from 1947 to 1963.PM Modi surpassed former prime minister Indira Gandhi, who delivered 11 consecutive Independence Day speeches between 1966 and 1976.PM Modi hoisted the National Flag at the Red Fort before beginning his address, with the ceremony synchronised with a 21-gun salute by the ceremonial battery.

Article Title: 'This is your last chance': SC ultimatum to Centre over delay in front-of-pack food warning labels
Article Text:
SC gave the government two weeks to take a final call on introducing warning labels for packaged foods.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday sharply criticised the Centre and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India FSSAI ) over the delay in introducing front-of-pack warning labels for packaged food products high in sugar, salt and saturated fat, warning that it would issue directions if the government failed to take a final decision.A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran gave the Centre two weeks to place its final decision on record, making it clear that the government could either implement the proposed warning labels on its own or face judicial intervention."This is your last chance. Next time we will dictate the judgment," the bench said, according to ANI.The court repeatedly underlined that the issue was one of public health, particularly the health of children and questioned the government's reluctance to move ahead with stronger nutritional warnings."Why? You don't want people of this country to remain healthy? More particularly growing children?" the bench asked during the hearing.Appearing for the Centre, additional solicitor general Brijender Chahar argued that applying strict warning standards could create complications for traditional Indian food items. He said products such as namkeen could end up carrying red warning symbols because of their fat or salt content.He also argued that international nutritional standards might not be directly applicable to Indian dietary habits, pointing out that even two eggs could exceed the prescribed daily fat limit.The court, however, was unconvinced.The bench said consumers were already aware that packaged foods contained sugar, fat and carbohydrates, but front-of-pack warning labels would provide a simpler and more effective way of communicating nutritional risks before a purchase was made.The judges also rejected the argument that warning labels could adversely affect manufacturers.According to ANI, the bench observed that the final decision to purchase a product would continue to rest with consumers and that commercial considerations could not take precedence over public health.During the proceedings, senior advocate Maninder Singh, appearing for a manufacturer, attempted to make submissions. The court responded by stating that the case concerned the health of citizens and that manufacturers could not determine government policy on the issue.Senior advocate Devadutt Kamat suggested that food products could be categorised differently and that detailed nutritional information should be displayed.The bench clarified that it was not opposed to any particular food product but was only seeking greater consumer awareness."In this country, how many people can afford dry fruits? And how many children buy Kurkure? That makes all the difference. We are not against any particular product. We only want the person purchasing it to know what he is consuming," the court said, according to ANI.The bench also referred to its February 10, 2026, order, in which it had previously addressed the issue and laid down its observations.During Thursday's hearing, the petitioner's counsel drew the court's attention to the minutes of an FSSAI meeting held on March 7, which allegedly reflected a position contrary to the suggestions made by the court earlier.The judges also took exception to the Centre's argument that India could not easily adopt international standards relating to nutritional warnings."We do not approve the stance of the Union when it says that it's not possible to match the international standards, more particularly developed countries. Should India remain an undeveloped country?" the bench asked, according to ANI."The world should know that India is concerned about the health of its citizens and more particularly children," it added.The case stems from a petition seeking mandatory front-of-pack warning labels for packaged food products containing high levels of sugar, salt and saturated fat.The proposed labels are intended to help consumers quickly identify potentially unhealthy products before buying them.The issue has also been discussed by Parliament's Committee on Subordinate Legislation, headed by Shiv Sena Rajya Sabha MP Milind Deora, who has advocated studying Singapore's Nutri-Grade model as a possible template for India.Separately, the Union health ministry has proposed displaying "sugar and oil boards" in schools, offices and other public institutions as part of a broader effort to encourage healthier eating habits and reduce excessive consumption of sugar and oil.
Article Summary: Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran gave the Centre two weeks to place its final decision on record. The court repeatedly underlined that the issue was one of public health, particularly the health of children. The proposed labels are intended to help consumers quickly identify potentially unhealthy products.

Article Title: Harsimrat Kaur Badal 'deeply touched' by PM Modi's 'kind gesture' after attack on Sukhbir Badal
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal on Friday said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief, Sukhbir Singh Badal , who was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.This marked the Badal family's first reaction to the attack on the former Punjab deputy chief minister."Truly grateful, Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji, for your personal call to inquire about Sardar Sukhbir Singh Badal ji’s health and for your good wishes for his speedy recovery following the dastardly attack on him inside a Gurudwara Sahib in Nanded, Maharashtra," Harsimrat Badal, SAD's only Lok Sabha MP, wrote on X.She also thanked the prime minister for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with the state police in the probe."Your concern, support and wishes during this difficult time mean a lot to all of us in the family, our party and to the people of Punjab. I am deeply touched by your kind gesture. I am also grateful to you for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with Maharashtra Police in the probe," the Bathinda MP added.On Thursday, Sukhbir Singh Badal was injured after being attacked by a kirpan-wielding assailant while leaving the Mata Sahib Devaji Gurdwara at Mudkhed in Maharashtra’s Nanded district. The assailant was arrested at the spot.Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis ordered an inquiry into the attack and spoke to Sukhbir Singh Badal over the phone. The SAD president is learnt to have told Fadnavis that he was stable, ANI reported.Earlier, Badal was also targeted in an attempted shooting at the Golden Temple in Amritsar in December 2024 while he was performing “seva”. The attacker allegedly tried to fire at him but was overpowered before he could cause any harm.The 2024 attack took place while Badal was carrying out “seva” after the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority in Sikhism, declared him a “tankhaiya,” or guilty of religious misconduct, over decisions taken by the SAD-led Punjab government between 2007 and 2017.The SAD and BJP, which currently lead the governments at the Centre and in Maharashtra, are former allies. In 2020, the SAD ended its alliance with the BJP in protest against the Centre’s contentious farm laws, which were later withdrawn.Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week, triggering speculation that the former allies could reunite ahead of the Punjab assembly elections early next year.
Article Summary: Harsimrat Kaur Badal said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief. Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday expressed “strong disapproval” of the Bar Council of India’s (BCI) now-revoked order barring the enrolment of 2026 graduates of Hyderabad’s NALSAR University of Law as advocates after a section of students objected to the university inviting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as the chief guest at its convocation ceremony.Kant, heading a bench also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said students have a right to protest peacefully and described the episode as a “dialogue” between him and the students."If students are protesting peacefully, who is BCI to take action? It is the right of the students to protest peacefully. It is a dialogue between students and me. No one else has to step in," the CJI said.Expressing its strong disapproval, the Supreme Court also stayed any coercive action against students or faculty by BCI or state Councils."It (the letter) was absolutely uncalled for," the bench added.The bench posted the matter for hearing after two weeks.On Thursday, the BCI had directed all state bar councils not to enrol any 2026 graduate of NALSAR University of Law as an advocate until further orders. It withdrew the directive within hours following an uproar on social media.In its initial statement, BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra said the council was examining allegations regarding a campaign against CJI Kant’s participation in the university’s convocation and had sought a report identifying those responsible.The BCI later modified its decision and allowed state bar councils to enrol the university’s 2026 graduates as advocates before withdrawing the notification altogether.The revised notification stated that the “vast majority” of students were innocent and should not be made to suffer for the alleged “misconduct” of a few.Around 450 graduating students of NALSAR had urged the university to reconsider inviting CJI Kant as chief guest, citing his alleged refusal to hear pleas concerning “police brutality” against students who had marched to Parliament on July 20 seeking the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG question paper leak in May. Pradhan’s resignation on July 25 brought the protests to an end.
Article Summary: Supreme Court expresses "strong disapproval" of Bar Council of India's now- revoked order. BCI had barred enrolment of 2026 graduates of Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law as advocates. Students objected to university inviting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as the chief guest at its convocation ceremony.

Article Title: Phuket plunge: Airbus sends initial report to AI, seeks maintenance details
Article Text:
Airbus has asked Air In- dia to carry out multiple tests and share the aircraft’s recent maintenance activi- ties as it continues its event assessment

NEW DELHI: “The elevators (control up and down movement of aircraft) and ailerons (controls left and right movement) surfaces were lost for around four seconds.” Airbus, in its initial assessment of the A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi on Aug 4, said the aircraft experienced a sudden loss in altitude that left 24 injured.“Based on analysis of the DFDR (digital flight data recorder),” Airbus found that within seven seconds between 9:32:44 am and 9:32:51 am, there was a loss of hydraulics systems — pressurised fluids which enable flight controls to move. At this point, the autopilot was disconnected and the aircraft’s nose went up (increase in pitch). All timings are in IST.The Airbus preliminary communication sent to AI on Aug 10 says “at (9:32:46 am) auto pilot 2 was disconnected, and full nose down (pitch down) input began being applied on first officer side with no direct response from the flight control surfaces” due to the loss of hydraulics. Five seconds later, a single hydraulic system was recovered and a few seconds later the remaining two systems were back, leading to recovery of normal flight control.Airbus has asked Air India to carry out multiple tests and share the aircraft’s recent maintenance activities as it continues its event assessment. “Since load exceedances were detected during the sudden altitude change, (maintenance) inspections must be performed.Please provide the inspection results once they are completed. Please provide more detailed pilot reports from the reported event clarifying what it is observed during the event,” the communication says.“...this event requires an analysis considering both aircraft systems and structural integrity, as airframe may have been affected by the movement,” it adds.While probe is on by Airbus and France’s accident investigator under the ambit of India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau, several pilots are questioning why Air India decided to fly the aircraft all the way to Delhi after it had recovered from the technical events.
Article Summary: Airbus has asked Air India to carry out multiple tests and share the aircraft’s recent maintenance activities. Airbus, in its initial assessment of the A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi on Aug 4, said the aircraft experienced a sudden loss in altitude that left 24 injured.

Article Title: Park outside your Bengaluru home? It may soon cost up to Rs 25,000 a year
Article Text:
Bengaluru plans to introduce paid annual permits for on-street residential parking (File photo enhanced with AI)

Rules propose

Private operators to enforce rules

Common parking portal planned

Penalties prescribed

Illegal parking on roads

Rs 500 for cars

Rs 300 for two-wheelers

Parking on footpaths

Rs 1,000 for cars

Rs 600 for two-wheelers

Key conditions

Residential street parking allowed only through permit

Permit valid for one year

Parking outside the permitted area will be treated as a violation





BENGALURU: The city is all set to put a price on one of its most contested public resources, road space.Under the proposed Greater Bengaluru Authority Parking Rules, 2026, residents who want to park their cars on the road outside their homes will have to obtain annual permits, with fees varying by vehicle type.The draft also proposes sweeping restrictions on where vehicles can be parked, particularly around major roads and Metro stations.There are proposals for a complete ban on parking on arterial roads identified as high-density corridors by Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).It also seeks parking restrictions during peak hours on select arterial roads notified by traffic police.In addition, vehicles would not be allowed to park near junctions, bus stops, transit hubs, pedestrian crossings and footpaths, with detailed setback requirements prescribed under the rules.The proposed rules seek to significantly reduce on-street parking near public transport hubs.Initially, on-street parking would be prohibited within 150 metres of Metro and suburban railway station boundaries. The draft allows city corporations to gradually increase the no-parking zone up to 500 metres.The proposal is expected to impact several high-footfall Metro station areas across the city where commuters currently rely on adjoining roads for parking.In a shift from the current system, the draft proposes to authorise private operators managing public parking facilities to issue violation notices, collect parking-related charges, tow vehicles and clamp vehicles after being formally authorised by city corporations.The operators would be required to record video evidence of violations before towing vehicles, and all towing activities would be overseen by traffic police.To increase organised parking supply, the draft allows city corporations to lease vacant private plots and develop them into public parking facilities.Private landowners who voluntarily convert vacant plots into parking facilities would be eligible for incentives, including property tax exemptions.Owners providing mechanised or multi-level parking facilities could receive 100% exemption from property tax and service charges, while owners offering surface-level parking could receive a 50% exemption.The draft directs Metro, BMTC and suburban rail agencies to create off-street parking facilities on land available with them, particularly at interchange stations and peripheral locations, to encourage park-and-ride travel.Transit agencies may also offer discounted parking rates for commuters using public transport.All parking operators, city corporations and transit agencies would be required to share real-time information on parking availability, occupancy and pricing with GBA.The data would eventually be integrated into a common citywide parking portal and mobile application to help motorists locate available parking spaces and enable authorities to plan future parking infrastructure.Traffic police will continue to have powers to enforce no-parking regulations, tow vehicles and take action against repeat offenders.The draft also allows city corporations to increase parking rates based on demand and location and proposes higher charges for longer parking durations to discourage all-day occupation of valuable road space.
Article Summary: Bengaluru plans to introduce paid annual permits for on-street residential parking. Residents will have to obtain annual permits, with fees varying by vehicle type. The draft also proposes sweeping restrictions on where vehicles can be parked, particularly around major roads and Metro stations.

2014: The tradition begins

NEW DELHI: To mark India’s 80th Independence Day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived at the Red Fort on Saturday wearing a striking red tie-and-dye turban with a long trailing end, as he delivered his 13th consecutive Independence Day address from the historic ramparts.The turban featured intricate red, green and white patterns, reflecting styles associated with Rajasthani and Gujarati traditions. He paired it with a white kurta-pajama and a brown jacket, completing the look with three pocket squares in saffron, white and green—the colours of the national flag.For more than a decade, PM Modi’s Independence Day appearances at the Red Fort have featured a closely watched visual tradition: the turban. Since his first address as Prime Minister in 2014, he has chosen safas and turbans in a wide range of colours, patterns and regional styles, often bringing India’s rich textile heritage and craftsmanship into focus.From Rajasthan’s bandhej and leheriya to tricolour-inspired designs, his choice of headgear has evolved from year to year while retaining its traditional character. Here is a look back at the distinctive turbans that have become a recognisable feature of Modi’s Independence Day appearances.For the 79th Independence Day, Modi opted for an all-saffron safa, paired with a white kurta and churidar, a saffron bandhgala jacket and a tricolour stole.The saffron turban marked his 12th consecutive Independence Day address from the historic Red Fort.In 2024, Modi chose a leheriya-print turban featuring bold orange, dark green and yellow streaks, with a long, deeply pleated tail.Leheriya is a traditional Rajasthani tie-dye textile known for its wave-like patterns, inspired by the movement of desert winds.Also read: 80th Independence Day: 'Vande Mataram' played for first time as PM Modi addresses nation Modi wore a multicoloured Rajasthani-style bandhani turban in 2023, featuring shades of yellow, green and red. The Prime Minister paired it with an off-white kurta-churidar, a black V-neck jacket and a geometric-patterned pocket square.In 2022, Modi aligned his Independence Day attire with the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign, wearing a white turban decorated with saffron and green stripes. He paired it with a white kurta-churidar and a baby-blue Nehru jacket.The headgear mirrored the colours of the national flag while retaining the traditional format associated with his Independence Day appearances.During the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021, Modi wore a saffron turban featuring bold red patterns and a long pink trail. He paired it with a white kurta, fitted churidar, deep blue jacket and a white scarf edged with a saffron border.The long trailing end remained a prominent feature of the headgear, continuing the distinctive visual style of his earlier Independence Day turbans.At the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, Modi chose a saffron-and-cream turban with an extended tail. He wore it with a white kurta and churidar, along with an orange-and-white stole that also served as a protective face covering.The ensemble combined his recurring use of traditional headgear with a practical response to the public-health circumstances of the time.In 2019, Modi wore a multicoloured safa featuring Rajasthan’s traditional leheriya wave pattern. The design created a ripple effect across the headgear and continued his use of regional textile traditions for the Independence Day occasion.In 2018, Modi returned to saffron, wearing a bright turban decorated with red patterns and a long trail that extended almost to his ankles.He paired the headgear with a white stole featuring a broad geometric-patterned border.Modi chose a vibrant yellow turban in 2017, featuring intricate traditional and geometric patterns woven across the fabric.The headgear combined bright red and yellow with a subtle golden criss-cross design.Also read: From bandhani to leheriya: PM Modi’s Independence Day turbans over the years In 2016, Modi embraced the classic tie-and-dye technique with a vibrant bandhej turban in bright pink and yellow. The headgear featured distinctive patterns and a long trailing end.The festive design reflected the Prime Minister’s preference for colourful traditional headgear during the Independence Day celebrations.In 2015, Modi wore a sunny yellow turban covered in a multicoloured criss-cross pattern combining red and deep green. The headgear featured a long trail extending towards his ankles, giving the traditional Rajasthani-style turban a prominent silhouette.It marked another early example of Modi using Independence Day attire to foreground Indian textile traditions.For his maiden Independence Day address as Prime Minister in 2014, Modi wore a bright red Jodhpuri bandhej turban with contrasting green accents.The Rajasthani-style headgear featured vivid orange, yellow and green tones and traditional patterns. That first Red Fort appearance established the colourful turban as a recurring element of Modi’s Independence Day wardrobe, a tradition that has continued through successive addresses.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi arrived at the Red Fort on Saturday wearing a striking red tie- and-dye turban. The turban featured intricate red, green and white patterns, reflecting styles associated with Rajasthani and Gujarati traditions. Since his first address as Prime Minister in 2014, he has chosen safas and turbans in a wide range of colours and patterns.

Article Title: In response to Pak PM Sharif, J&K CM Omar says IWT sucked ‘our blood’, calls for its cancellation
Article Text:
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SRINAGAR: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned at an event in Islamabad on Friday that Pakistan would take any step to protect its water rights under the Indus Waters Treaty , saying “every single drop” of Pakistan’s water is a “red line” and “India must come to the right path” or it would “be given a direct response”. His comments drew a reaction from Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah who said the treaty has been kept in abeyance and should remain so.“Yes, our blood. We have been saying this only, that our blood has been sucked. Thankfully Shehbaz Sharif came to his senses. This (IWT) has sucked the blood out of us. These are our rivers. We have the first right on them,” Omar told reporters here. “For the sake of saying, Pakistanis say that they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was his sympathy when our permission to use our rivers was taken away from us,” the CM said.“Out of the six rivers, three which belonged to Punjab were kept by India and our three rivers were handed over to Pakistan. From then till today we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,” Omar said, adding that under the treaty J&K could neither extract drinking water from the Chenab nor use the Jhelum for irrigation or building a barrage at Tulbul. “Our blood has been sucked and now the IWT has been cancelled.This should remain cancelled so that we can use this water properly,” Omar added.The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. In May last year, after the treaty was placed in abeyance, Omar called for restarting the Tulbul Navigation Project on Wular Lake in north Kashmir. The project is located on Wular Lake in the Sopore area of Baramulla district. Pakistan has opposed construction of a 439-foot-long, 40-foot-wide barrage, also known as the Wular barrage or Tulbul Navigation Project, with a navigation lock on the lake.The Union govt began work on the project in 1984 to regulate water levels and facilitate navigation. However, work was halted a year later after Pakistan objected. Pakistan raised the issue with the Indus Waters Commission in 1986 and work was stopped in 1987.The governing National Conference in J&K has opposed the IWT all along, calling it detrimental to the interests of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
Article Summary: India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers. Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.

Article Title: CJI, Nalsar students have one query for BCI: ‘Who are you?’
Article Text:
The apex court bench sought BCI’s explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions

SC asks bar council to explain process behind resolutions against students

The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression CJI Surya Kant

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Friday castigated the Bar Council of India (BCI) for threatening to deny licence to practice to Hyderabad-based NALSAR university students who opposed CJI Surya Kant as their convocation chief guest, shielded them against coercive action, and offered the law graduates a start as legal aid counsel in SC.Taking cognisance of the controversy created late Thursday evening by BCI through an unprecedented letter which had to be hastily retracted, a three-judge bench led by CJI Surya Kant said, “This is absolutely uncalled for. BCI has nothing to do with it. The students might have written a letter to me. It is a dialogue between me and students. Who are they (BCI) to unnecessarily create an issue? This action is totally uncalled for. ”Senior advocate K Parameshwar sought SC’s urgent intervention in quashing the illegal and arbitrary action of the BCI in seeking to coerce VC of NALSAR University, one of the top law schools, to conduct an investigation and identify students who had opposed CJI’s participation in the convocation as chief guest and issuing the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practice by all state bar councils.Trashing Bar Council of India’s threat to blackball protesting Nalsar students, CJI Surya Kant told senior advocate K Parameshwar to convey to the students, who are completing their graduation in law from Nalsar this year, “to get licences to practice at the earliest and begin their careers in Supreme Court”.The apex court bench sought BCI’s explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions prior to issuing a letter to bar licences to protesters, and another shortly after, retracting it.Urging the students to join the SC bar at the earliest, the CJI said, “We will empanel them and give them legal aid cases. This will be our response to all those who intend to create impediments in their professional career.”He added, “We should be largehearted. Even if someone makes a wrong statement at a young age, let it rest there. That does not mean they do not have a right to speak.”“During my student days, I was actively involved in many student activities. Indulging in activities or protests does not mean the students are wrong. The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. So long as they are lawfully and peacefully raising their voice over an issue, it must be heard, not opposed. Unnecessarily, Bar Council of India meddled in it.Neither BCI nor any other body has any business to interfere with this,” said the CJI.Earlier, the advocate had raised the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practise by all state bar councils.The CJI-led bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, without even going through the petition by two formerstudents of Nalsar, restrained BCI and all state bar councils from taking any coercive or punitive action against the students and faculty.Accepting the notice on behalf of BCI, advocate Radhika Gautam said the objectionable circular had been withdrawn. In its order, the Supreme Court asked Bar Council of India to file its counter-affidavit in two weeks.
Article Summary: Bar Council of India (BCI) threatened to deny licence to practice to Hyderabad- based NALSAR university students who opposed CJI Surya Kant as their convocation chief guest. The apex court bench sought BCI’s explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions.

The FDA issued 60 improvement notices and ordered one facility to temporarily halt operations, news agency PTI reported.Of the 14 suspended licences, five were linked to Blinkit, five to Zepto, two to Instamart, while one each belonged to Bhagwati Stores and Swinsta Ent Pvt Ltd.The inspections focused on storage conditions, temperature control, cleanliness, pest management, personal hygiene of food handlers, food safety records, display of licences and compliance with inventory practices such as First In, First Out (FIFO) and First Expired, First Out (FEFO).In Pune, the FDA suspended the licence of a Zepto outlet in Lohegaon after inspectors found food items stored beyond their declared "use by" dates.The regulator also flagged unhygienic storage conditions, inadequate pest control and lapses in personal hygiene, adding that the company's response during the hearing was unsatisfactory.Another Pune facility operated by Swinsta Ent Pvt Ltd was found to have a cockroach infestation, inadequate cold-chain maintenance for frozen products and deficiencies in hygiene and pest-control practices.In Mumbai, a Blinkit facility in Malad (West) was found to be operating with chiller temperatures above the prescribed limit. Inspectors also found that around 40 food handlers had not undergone mandatory medical examinations and that records were unavailable.The FDA said several workers were not using protective gear such as gloves, aprons and head coverings. Inspectors also found damaged storage racks, poor organisation and inadequate segregation of different categories of food products.At another Blinkit facility in Ghatkopar, officials flagged shortcomings in drainage, waste disposal, temperature control and housekeeping. The outlet was classified as non-compliant after scoring 46 per cent during the inspection.Inspections at Zepto facilities in Mulund and Goregaon revealed deficiencies related to food storage, temperature management, cleanliness and licence display.At an Instamart outlet in Andheri, inspectors found food packets stored directly on the floor. The FDA also reported inadequate storage space, overcrowding and deficiencies in hygiene and temperature control.The inspection drive also covered delivery operations.At a Blinkit store in Karad in Satara district, officials checked 125 delivery riders and found that they lacked identity cards and medical fitness records. The regulator also found that the outlet's FSSAI licence was not displayed on delivery bags and boxes.The FDA directed the company to suspend two-wheeler delivery operations at the outlet until the deficiencies were addressed.The regulator said the action was taken under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and urged all food businesses operating through online platforms to strictly comply with prescribed food safety, hygiene and storage standards.
Article Summary: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the licences of 14 food business establishments linked to quick-commerce platforms Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. Inspections uncovered violations ranging from cockroach infestation and expired food to poor hygiene and storage practices.

Article Title: 40 queries in Census Phase-II: Caste, bank accounts, Covid jabs...
Article Text:
Data will remain confidential, can’t be used for legal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosure

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The second phase of Census 2027 — involving population enumeration, will, for the first time, capture caste “as declared by the respondent” among its 40 fields, which include new ones such as number of bank accounts, place of Covid vaccination and voter card number.Enumeration by caste will not delve into the question of whether it falls under other backward classes (OBC) category. However, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes will be enumerated as earlier, with all notified SC/ST communities listed in the drop-down menus.In a first, the questionnaire notified Friday for the upcoming population enumeration phase of Census 2027, shall seek the name of the spouse, parents’ particulars and nationality — elements captured by the national population register ( exercise undertaken alongside Census 2011 and proposed to be repeated with Census 2021 before the latter was postponed due to Covid. NPR updation was however delinked from Census 2027.The Phase 2 questionnaire lists 40 questions, up from 29 asked during Census 2011. The new fields include, apart from caste, spouse’s name and mother and father’s particulars, the respondent’s nationality as declared, permanent address, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number and availability of driving license.While the mobile number, Aadhaar no and voter ID may be shared if available, the passport number is required only from an Indian passport holder.Sources told TOI that mother and father’s particulars are likely to capture their names, date of birth and place of birth. While these are key factors that determine citizenship/nationality, their capture will have no impact on individuals since individual census data must remain confidential and cannot be used for “legal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosure,” as per the govt. A senior govt functionary said the aggregate data, however, may give a picture of overall population that meets the citizenship criteria as per the Citizenship Act.TOI was the first to report on August 3 that the Phase 2 questionnaire shall capture caste “as declared by the respondent” and, in a first, also capture parents’ date and place of birth.Sources said that giving the drop down option for enumeration was not found to be feasible because states have different classes categorised as OBCs, with mismatch between the communities recognised as such by the Centre and those at the level of states. Sources also pointed to the trend of states expanding their respective OBC lists by adding more castes/classes, something which could have created logistical problems once the Census was underway.Officials told TOI that unlike the socio-economic caste census conducted in 2011 — which had returned around 46 lakh castes, making it unusable — the digital mode of Census 2027 and availability of modern, AI-based tools can surmount compilation and segregation challenges. Also, the full confidentiality of an individual’s caste declaration is guaranteed by the Census Act.In other shifts from previous census exercises, the fertility data to be collected in Census 2027 will skip the differentiation between male and female children. Also, literacy status will separately capture digital literacy.Even though an individual’s aadhaar no, voter ID and passport details enumerated as part of census cannot be disclosed to any entity, including govt departments, sources said the data, when aggregated, can give the big picture on coverage of these documents and identify the gaps. Similarly, the number of bank accounts will give an idea of the penetration and distribution of banking services.Phase 2 is due to start in Union territory of Ladakh and the snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of J&K, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh on August 17; self-enumeration window will run from August 17 to 31, followed by field enumeration from Sept 1 to 30. For the rest of the country, the population enumeration will resume in February 2027, culminating in the population headcount with March 1, 2027, as the reference date.Phase 1 of Census is due to be completed across the country by Sept 30, 2026.Among the usual fields included in the Phase 2 questionnaire are religion, age at marriage, disability, mother tongue and other spoken languages, education, occupation and migration.
Article Summary: The Phase 2 questionnaire lists 40 questions, up from 29 asked during Census 2011. The new fields include, apart from caste, spouse’s name and mother and father's particulars. Data will remain confidential, can’t be used for legal evidence, govt benefits or public disclosure.

Article Title: On Independence Day, TOI talks to Gandhi, Bose & Nehru
Article Text:

'Names bring history into an ordinary life'

In classrooms of generations past, an attendance register could sometimes sound like a roll call from India's freedom movement. Many parents named their children after national heroes. Today, those names are hard to find. But you can still come across a Gandhi, Nehru or Bose.Take Hyderabad's Jawaharlal Nehru . Born in the 1960s to freedom fighter and Congress member Mutteswara Rao, Nehru says his father was determined on the name of India's first PM. Rao reached out to him.The PMO pointed out Nehru was a surname and suggested the child be named Jawahar. But Rao was adamant."Being Jawaharlal Nehru, I feel, needs commitment," he says. He encouraged his only son to join the Army. "I stand for the country. I can proudly say my son is a Major."My father insisted he had a letter from Nehru giving his permission. That's how I became Jawaharlal Nehru," says the man who now heads Telangana govt's Tele-MANAS Centre. Nehru's sister, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, also has a modern-day namesake in Hyderabad. She was originally named Vijayalakshmi by her mother.Her father, a freedom fighter, later added Pandit to her name after the original became president of United Nations General Assembly.For Subhas Chandra Bose , a 33-year-old employee of Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences, the name came with expectations from childhood. "Everyone told me I should not do anything mediocre or bad because of my name," he says. "I still feel that responsibility. I don't even lie." His father didn't stop with one famous name.Subhas' brothers are named Chandrasekhar Azad and Ambedkar.There's also CLN Gandhi, a retired additional commissioner in the transport department, known simply as Gandhi in bureaucratic circles. "My father named me after Mahatma Gandhi as suggested by our neighbour, who was in the Army," he says. "I was always conscious of the values associated with my name."Socio-political analyst S Ramakrishna said: "When a child is named after a historical figure, that memory travels with the person. The name brings history into an ordinary life."
Article Summary: Hyderabad's Jawaharlal Nehru says his father was determined on the name of India's first PM. Nehru's sister, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, also has a modern-day namesake in Hyderabad. For Subhas Chandra Bose, the name came with expectations from childhood.

Article Title: “Some day” is today
Article Text:
Thirukkural with the Times explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text ‘Thirukkural’. Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. This text is divided into three books with teachings on virtue, wealth, and love and is considered one of the great works ever on ethics and morality. The Kural has influenced scholars and leaders across social, political, and philosophical spheres.

Motivational speaker, author and diversity champion Bharathi Bhaskar explores the masterpiece.

Last week, our college friend group of eleven girls lost one of our own. Through our four years in college, we had become inseparable. Three decades later, we were still together.And then, Devi was no more.For two years, she fought cancer bravely. She was the first to wish us on birthdays and anniversaries. We would wake to find her messages, often at 5.30 in the morning. Her love was like dawn. It brightened the lives of all around her. Her smile seemed to rise from the altar of her heart.We wept. Yet, strangely, there is also a quiet peace in knowing that she may now be in a place without pain. Where that place is, none of us know. But perhaps the more important realisation is that all of us are travelling towards it, each at our own pace.Losing someone we love shakes up our lives. Guilt arrives uninvited, whispering about words left unsaid and things left undone. Then life, with its extraordinary insistence, pulls us back. There are mails to send, vessels to wash, clothes to fold, work to finish. We think we are moving on, until suddenly, it returns, and we are thrown back into the tide of longing.Perhaps that is because love does not leave as easily as a person does.And perhaps the people we have loved have not entirely left us. Are they watching us? Are they closer than before? Sometimes I imagine them as passengers who have quietly got down from the train before us, without the chance to say goodbye. We continue our journey, carrying their memories with us.Younger colleagues approach the world differently. At home, children no longer listen to us. But with school and college friends, time seems to freeze.That is our safe haven. When one of us leaves that circle, however, we suddenly become conscious of the passing years.Valluvar captured this truth with remarkable simplicity in Kural 334:“Naalena Ondrupol Kaatti, UyirerumVaaladhu Unarvaar Perin.”“Every day appears to be merely a day, but to those who understand, it is a sword quietly cutting away a portion of life.”In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira is asked by the Yaksha, “What is the strangest thing in the world?”He replies, “Countless beings leave the world every day, yet those who remain believe they will remain forever.” What greater wonder could there be?But perhaps this need not frighten us. It can awaken us, instead.Every day is a flower that blooms for exactly one day. The July rain, the December chill, the fragrance of neem in summer; all carry a beauty that will never return in precisely the same form.The lesson is not to fear the passing of days, but to live them fully. To laugh a little. To say what we keep postponing. To savour the morning light and coffee.Kahlil Gibran asks, “You want to know the secret of death. But how shall you find it unless you seek it in the heart of life?”That is where the answer lies.Not in knowing how the journey ends, but in making every day of the journey luminous.Devi did that for many of us. I will remember her; not as someone who has left, but as someone who taught us quietly how much radiance one life can leave behind.
Article Summary: Bharathi Bhaskar explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text ‘Thirukkural’ Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each.

A new phase of space exploration has been ushered in through the recent successful rocket launch by a young team with an average age of just 28 years,” the Murmu said. “Our younger generations strengthen my faith in India’s bright and prosperous future,” she added.The President also emphasised that physical and mental wellbeing of our youth forms the cornerstone of our country’s future. “Families and society also share the responsibility to motivate our youth to move ahead with enthusiasm,” she said.Reflecting on various issued during her address, the President, while noting that warfare and instability prevailing in several parts of the world are affecting every country, said that even in such trying circumstances, “according to economic projections, the growth rate of the Indian economy is expected to be more than twice the average global growth rate.”Mentioning that May 7 marked the completion of one year since the launch of Operation Sindoor, Murmu said, “That historic operation against terrorism sent a clear and firm message to terrorists and those who support them, that no matter where they hide, they will have to face the consequences of their actions.”Speaking in the context of Pakistan, the President said that the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty with "the country that harbours terrorism" is a decisive step in the interest of India, especially the farmers.

Jodhpur: In an embarrassing mix-up, Jodhpur zila parishad's chief executive officer, in his capacity as district election officer, Thursday issued a notice to Member of Parliament Manna Lal Rawat for negligence in election duties, mistakenly believing the latter still held a position as joint commissioner with the state transport department.The notice, which warned Rawat of potential disciplinary action due to a failure to update the list of his subordinate employees on the state govt's EMS (employee management system) portal in preparation for the upcoming municipal elections, was swiftly retracted following public ridicule on social media Friday.Rawat, who resigned from his state govt post prior to the 2024 general elections, is currently serving as a Lok Sabha member representing Udaipur on a BJP ticket. The goof-up occurred as a govt portal was not updated. Confirming this, Rawat said that district election officer (CEO, zila parishad) Ashish Kumar Mishra called him, admitted the mistake and withdrew the notice.Rawat was earlier posted as the transport department's joint commissioner in Jodhpur. He took voluntary retirement in 2024 to contest the parliamentary elections that year. Despite his retirement and subsequent election as a public representative, Rawat's name continued to figure in the list of govt employees maintained by the Jodhpur district election authorities.The error came to light after the notice was issued to him, raising questions over the way employee data is maintained and updated by the state election machinery. "It is surprising and worrisome," said Rawat, adding that despite the govt machinery operating in a digital environment, election-related data was still carrying information that was nearly three years old. Rawat questioned how govt departments were maintaining the data of ordinary citizens and serving employees if the records of a retired senior govt officer had not been removed from the list even after a considerable lapse of time.
Article Summary: Jodhpur zila parishad's chief executive officer issued a notice to Member of Parliament Manna Lal Rawat for negligence in election duties. He mistakenly believed the latter still held a position as joint commissioner with the state transport department. The notice was swiftly retracted following public ridicule on social media.

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) has called for nationwide protests on August 17 over a range of pending labour issues, including higher minimum pension, revision of EPF and ESI wage ceilings, restoration of the Old Pension Scheme and changes to provisions of the new labour codes.The organisation has asked all its units across the country to hold demonstrations, rallies and dharnas at district headquarters and submit memorandums to the Prime Minister, finance minister and labour minister. NEW DELHI: Television channels will no longer be restricted to 12 minutes of advertisements per hour, with the government deciding to scrap the two-decade-old cap in a move it says will put traditional broadcasters on a more level footing with digital platforms.The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the Gazette, the information and broadcasting ministry said.The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 TV channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now. Cable television, then the dominant distribution platform, was largely analog and offered limited capacity and consumer choice.With digitisation, platforms including cable TV, direct-to-home, HITS and IPTV can now carry 300 to 500 channels or more, significantly expanding viewer choice and competition, the ministry said.The decision could give broadcasters greater flexibility to determine advertising inventory, an important consideration for an industry that remains heavily dependent on advertising revenue across both pay and free-to-air channels.The ministry also cited the growing competition television faces from digital media, where there is no comparable statutory cap on advertising duration.It said the existing restriction had created a “non-level playing field” for conventional television broadcasters and that removing it would promote “fair competition” and ease of doing business.The change, however, will become operational only from the date the amendment to the Cable Television Networks Rules is formally notified.

Article Title: Pew survey: What US, UK and others think about India at 80
Article Text:

Neighbourhood contrasts & global scorecard

as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?

India's image is changing

Politics matters too

A mixed but largely positive global image

As India completes 79 years of independence, its global standing presents a striking study in contrasts.A Pew Research Center survey conducted across 36 countries between February and May 2026 reveals an international community divided down the middle: a global median of 45% of respondents hold a favorable view of India, while 41% express an unfavorable opinion.Behind this median lies a complex tapestry of geopolitical shifts, historical rivalries, and evolving regional alliances.From enthusiasm in Western Europe and East Africa to frosty hostility in parts of the Middle East and South Asia, public perception of the world’s most populous democracy depends heavily on where you ask.Nowhere is this divergence more intense than in India's immediate backyard. While proximity can foster cooperation, in South Asia it has produced antithetical attitudes.Sri Lanka has the most favourable view of India, with 79% of adults expressing a positive opinion.Pakistan sits at the opposite end, with just 7% viewing India favourably. The gulf between the two countries reflects decades of conflict, political rivalry and competing national narratives.Turkey is another major outlier. Only 15% of Turks have a favourable opinion of India, while a majority hold an unfavourable view.In the West Bank and East Jerusalem, just 18% express a positive opinion.Yet beyond these pockets of hostility, India finds considerable goodwill across much of the world.Kenya and the United Kingdom rank alongside Sri Lanka among the countries most positive towards India, with roughly seven in 10 adults expressing favourable views.Majorities in Germany, Israel, Italy, Sweden, Japan and Thailand also see India positively.In contrast, Latin American publics express mixed-to-negative views, alongside substantial shares of respondents who offer no opinion.The findings suggest that India's global image is not simply a reflection of its diplomatic alliances.Economic ties, strategic partnerships, cultural familiarity and perceptions of India's growing global role all appear to shape how people view the country.The bigger story is perhaps not where India stands today, but how its image has changed.In most countries surveyed, opinions have remained relatively stable since Pew last asked the question. But in 10 countries, the change has been statistically significant — and in seven of them, India's favourability has fallen.Turkey and Nigeria have recorded the sharpest declines since 2025, with the share of people expressing a favourable opinion of India falling by 10 percentage points in both countries.India has also lost ground in the United States, Indonesia, South Africa and Mexico.The decline is particularly striking in Bangladesh.Pew's previous survey there was conducted in 2024. Since then, the share of Bangladeshis with a favourable opinion of India has fallen by 15 percentage points, leaving fewer than half with a positive view.At the same time, the number of Bangladeshis who do not express an opinion has also fallen sharply, from 24% to just 7%. In other words, more Bangladeshis now appear to have a defined opinion of India — and that opinion has become considerably less favourable.The trend is not uniformly negative, however.India's image has improved significantly in Germany, Britain and Sri Lanka.The share of Britons with a favourable opinion of India has risen 11 points since 2025, while Germany has recorded a six-point increase. Sri Lanka has seen an even bigger jump, with favourability rising 14 points since 2024.Looking further back to 2023 reveals another interesting divide.Across several European countries, India's image has strengthened substantially since the first post-pandemic survey. In Germany, for example, only 47% had a favourable opinion of India in 2023. That figure has now climbed to 63%.France has followed a similar trajectory. India's favourability there has risen from 39% in 2023 to 50% today.Outside Europe, however, the picture is less encouraging.South Korea is one example. In 2023, 59% of South Koreans viewed India favourably. Today, that figure has dropped to 44%.Latin America also tends to lean more negative, although large numbers of people in several European and Latin American countries do not express an opinion at all.India's global image is also shaped by domestic political ideology in some countries.The United States and Canada show a striking pattern: people on the political left are more likely than conservatives to view India favourably.In the US, 54% of liberals express a positive opinion of India, compared with 40% of conservatives. In Canada, the corresponding figures are 58% and 45%.Israel presents almost the exact opposite picture.There, 68% of people on the political right view India favourably, compared with just 46% on the left.The ideological divide underlines how perceptions of India can be tied not only to India's own policies, but also to how different political constituencies interpret its role in the world.So, as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?The answer is neither uniformly celebratory nor overwhelmingly negative.Pakistan and Turkey may give India the stink eye, but they represent the more hostile end of a much broader spectrum.From Sri Lanka and Kenya to Britain, Germany and Israel, India enjoys strong positive sentiment in several strategically important countries.At the same time, the declines in Bangladesh, the US, South Korea, Turkey, Nigeria and other countries show that India's global image cannot be taken for granted.India's international reputation is therefore becoming more consequential — and more contested.As New Delhi seeks a larger role in global affairs, its challenge will not simply be to build economic and military power, but also to shape how that power is perceived abroad.At 80, India is increasingly a country the world has an opinion about.
Article Summary: A Pew Research Center survey conducted across 36 countries between February and May 2026 reveals an international community divided down the middle. A global median of 45% of respondents hold a favorable view of India, while 41% express an unfavorable opinion. In 10 countries, the change has been statistically significant — and in seven of them, India's favourability has fallen.

Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Yale's Vice Provost for International Affairs.He has received the 2016 Infosys Prize in Humanities, a 2017 MacArthur Fellowship, and the 2025 Toynbee Prize in Global History, among others. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'.It was a coming together of my academic life and the rest of my life. For close to 20 years, I had been researching some of the themes that do make it into 'The Burning Earth'. I've particularly been interested in the relationship between migration, the movement of people and environmental change. So I wrote a book more than 10 years ago called 'Crossing the Bay of Bengal', which I think was my first foray into environmental history, in which I was really thinking about the enormous movement of people, particularly from Tamil Nadu, to southeast Asia in the 19th and 20th century, many of them to work on rubber plantations, but also to work in port cities, places like Singapore and Penang and Rangoon, and understanding that that was actually a moment of fundamental transformation in the environment... At the same time, as a teacher, but also as a parent, as a citizen, the climate crisis became quite unavoidable in my own consciousness. And so for me, that prompted me to scale things up beyond my areas of specialisation towards perhaps the biggest question, which is how did we get to this point of planetary crisis? And that's really what's at the heart of 'The Burning Earth'.If the question is what is it about my own perspective that may make this book a little bit different from some of the other books out there on this big theme of the environment, it is the fact that my own training is not in European and North American history. And I think most of what is called global history continues to take as its starting point and as its default, a kind of familiar North Atlantic history. And so by starting the book in China and ending it in Indonesia, I was really trying to write it anchored in Asia. .. Asia has always been home to the majority of humanity. It still is today. And so it seemed to me completely fitting to really think about the history of this planet with a firm anchor in the part of the world, the part of the planet which has been the most inhabited by most people throughout the longest period of time.That's the biggest challenge of a book like this. There's no possibility that I can have the primary expertise in all of these areas that I write about in the book. And so in some ways that was a leap that I took. Academia is a collective enterprise. And this is very much a book that builds on my own work in some areas. And in other areas, it's really sort of bringing together my reading in multiple fields of scholarship and different disciplines as well. So I'm a historian, but some of the most exciting new scholarship which I draw on and interpret is actually coming from the physical sciences.There's some phenomenally interesting work in paleoclimatology, for example, which is trying to reconstruct past climates using ice cores, using lake bed sediment, using tree rings. And of course, these disciplines traditionally and even still within the walls of the university barely meet. But what's been very interesting about recent work on climate and environment in particular, is you have this forcing together of completely different ideas of what the archive is.I don't use the word that many times, but when I do, I think it's doing a lot of work for me. 'The Burning Earth' is not an activist book, which is to say that it is just that bit muddier and less clear about the villains of the piece than activist writing necessarily has to be. And yet there is such a strong core in my own thinking of awareness of just how stark environmental inequalities are and just how much the scale of planetary destruction that has been achieved over the last two centuries has been disproportionately, not exclusively, but disproportionately driven by the elite pursuit of luxuries and of accumulation. .. There is a story of human need in this book and there's also a story of human greed... I think we need to think about desire, we need to think about states, we need to think about liberation, we need to think about the genuinely liberatory promises that led to some of this environmental destruction which can't be reduced to a question of greed or even of capitalism...There's no question that the social and economic system that has been a driving force in the climate crisis is the capitalist system. But the socialist system in some sense was even more environmentally profligate and wasteful. It was just less successful. And so in terms of its longevity, in terms of the scale on which it was operating, it kind of doesn't compare with what a particular capitalist mode of production does to our ability to treat all of nature as commodity and to lead to this kind of constantly expanding frontier of production.But my question is really a different one, which is, where were the alternatives? Who was thinking differently?I think that's one of the key narratives in the book to show that the moments of the most intensive and accelerated environmental destruction over the last several hundred years have almost always gone together with moments of intense violence. And violence is at the core of 'The Burning Earth'. Not just violence against the earth or against nature, but against other people... Wars that are going on all around us in the world today are part of a very long pattern where armed violence and militarism and military destruction have been inextricably bound with massive environmental destruction.
Article Summary: Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'
